#5552. U.S. Army Triggers Massive Lead-Explosive Blast in Iowa as Locals Brace for Potentially Toxic Plume

The U.S. Army plans to detonate 9,700 pounds of a lead-based explosive in Southeast Iowa on Wednesday, despite concerns from environmental groups.

The U.S. army has detonated 9,7000 pounds of a lead-based explosive in Southeast Iowa on Wednesday after warning that the bomb-making chemicals had degraded and could be explosive.

The controlled detonated of the country's entire stockpile of the explosive was carried out at at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, IA at 10am EST.

After the detonation, local news station KWQC reported seeing a large plume of smoke.

Gov. Kim Reynolds said the detonation was a success.

“I want to commend Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle, Army leadership, and the skilled soldiers who planned and executed a flawless detonation this morning at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant and express my gratitude to the Trump Administration for its whole-of-government response," she said.

The detonation came after a lawsuit was filed by the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club Iowa Chapter asking the federal appeals court to halt the plan.

Two rapid, controlled detonations were initially scheduled to take place last Friday, but the plans were pushed to Wednesday due to a combination of public concern and weather optimization.

Set to be detonated are 68 drums of degraded lead azide, adding up to roughly 9,700 pounds, which have become sensitive and unstable. It is the primary explosive used to initiate munitions

A controlled detonation is now the only viable option, according to the Army’s Q&A page about the event.

As lead azide degrades, it crystalizes and becomes sensitive to temperature changes, shock, and friction, making it unsafe to move. There are chemical neutralization procedures, but the drums are too unstable for the physical manipulation this option requires, according to the Army.

U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Region 7 Director Jim Macy wrote a letter to Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds, ensuring her that the EPA was working alongside the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the Department of Defense to ensure the controlled detonation was “conducted in the safest manner possible.”

“All agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized,” Macy wrote in the letter, according to the Iowa Capital Dispatch.

An updated public safety advisory shared by the Army on Tuesday shared the agency’s plans to make the detonation as safe as possible. The lead azide will be detonated in earth-covered magazines, which are built for the purposes of holding ammunition and explosives, and are reinforced.

Additional physical barriers made of sand, a “water wall,” gel blocks, and aqueous foam barriers will be in place to contain particle dispersion, absorb thermal energy, and reduce airborne particulate dispersal. These measures, as well as drone surveillance of lead levels, are in place to track and minimize deposition outside the plant.

The Army has acknowledged that lead particles will impact communities outside the plant. It has defined an evacuation zone as a "5-mile cone extending southwest of IAAAP."

Those in the evacuation zone will be provided short-term hotel lodging, food, water, and transportation as needed.

It has also laid out recommendations for those outside the evacuation zone, such as sheltering in place, closing all windows and doors, and setting heating to recirculate and avoid pulling in air from outside.

Still, environmental groups are concerned about the lead plume, which they say could spread 100 miles, depending on weather conditions.

"The EPA itself admits that there is no safe level of lead exposure for humans," said Michael Schmidt, general counsel at the Iowa Environmental Council, in a press release shared with Realtor.com®.

"When our federal government makes decisions that result in a potentially toxic plume of lead dust that could cover much of southeastern Iowa, Iowans deserve to know that every available alternative was considered before choosing this method of disposal."

The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, Iowa Chapter, were only made aware of the unprecedented detonation plan early last week, initially scheduled for Friday. In response, the groups filed a lawsuit on Thursday challenging the permit that the EPA issued the Army.

“Based on the information that was made public at the time, which was very little information, there were serious concerns about the effectiveness of the public notification and the information being put out to protect the public,” Thien Chau, a senior attorney at Earth Justice, tells Realtor.com.

“There were serious concerns about the mitigations measures in place to reduce the impact as well as to properly do remediation and cleanup and address any harm that people may face from the impact of the detonation.”

Many local lawmakers were not made aware of the controlled detonation either, and were only informed about the plans and risk once the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra club told them, despite the widespread impact on surrounding communities, according to Chau.

“That’s why we filed the lawsuit: to make sure that all the information and resources and capabilities that could be provided were provided to the people potentially impacted by this,” says Chau.

“Since that filing, a lot of things have happened. The government has put out a lot more information, and while we expect a detonation to take place this Wednesday, we are glad to see that because there was additional time, there are now additional mitigation measures and resources have been provided for potentially impacted people.”

The Department of Justice responded in opposition to the lawsuit. Both the DOJ and Army maintain that a controlled detonation is the safest option and further delay, especially with cold weather approaching, could lead to a natural, uncontrolled detonation, which would be more difficult to mitigate.

“The Army has delayed detonation by three days now,” the DOJ’s brief said. “But every day of delay increases the risk of an uncontrolled explosion that will cause far greater public health and environmental harm than the planned, controlled detonation initiated under the protective terms of the Permit.”

#5551. STAT+: Medicare estimates $9.2 billion in savings from third round of negotiated drug prices

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

John Wilkerson, a Washington correspondent, is the author of D.C. Diagnosis, a twice-weekly newsletter about the politics and policy of health and medicine.

John writes about the politics of health care, and he is the author of the twice-weekly D.C. Diagnosis newsletter. You can reach John on Signal at John_Wilkerson.07.

WASHINGTON — The Trump administration on Monday said that the federal government will save $9.2 billion on drugs purchased through Medicare next year as a result of price negotiations, a net savings of 45% compared to what it would’ve paid last year had the negotiated prices been in effect.

This is the third time the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has negotiated drug prices following the passage of the Inflation Reduction Act, but it’s the first time those drugs have included treatments administered in doctors’ offices, which are covered by Part B. Only retail drugs covered by Part D were eligible during the first two years.

The estimated $9.2 billion in savings does not account for discounts the drugmakers pay to the Part D Manufacturer Discount Program. That program was created by the same law that established the price negotiation program. If those discounts were included, the estimated savings would be about $5.5 billion, or 33% in lower net aggregate spending.

#5550. Cannabis addiction linked to 57% higher odds of suicidal thoughts

As marijuana becomes more widely available and accepted, researchers are uncovering important questions about its effects on mental health. A major new study suggests that people who struggle to control their cannabis use face a substantially greater likelihood of experiencing suicidal thoughts.

Published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research found that adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting suicidal thoughts compared with those without the condition. Despite major shifts in marijuana laws and public attitudes, this troubling association remained remarkably consistent over a decade.

The findings come from an analysis of more than 415,000 American adults who participated in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health. Researchers examined data collected between 2014 and 2023, a period when cannabis became increasingly accessible across the United States.

"What surprised me most was not that cannabis use disorder was associated with suicidal thoughts, but that this association did not appear to strengthen over time," said lead author Tosin Philip Oyetunji, MPH, a doctoral student in public health at the University of California, Merced. "[Yet,] it remains an important mental health concern that deserves attention."

Cannabis and Suicidal Thoughts Show a Persistent Link

The connection between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thinking was observed across different age groups, sexes, and racial and ethnic backgrounds. However, women and younger adults showed particularly elevated risks.

Importantly, the association remained even after researchers accounted for depression, psychological distress, and other factors that could influence mental health outcomes.

The consistency of the results was especially notable given how dramatically the cannabis landscape has changed. Recreational marijuana is now legal in half of U.S. states, and cannabis products have become increasingly potent. These developments have raised concerns among public health experts about whether broader access might contribute to worsening mental health.

Yet the study offers some reassurance on that particular question. Sidra Goldman-Mellor, PhD, a professor of public health at UC Merced and the study's senior author, noted that the association between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thoughts did not become stronger during the 10 years examined.

"Suicidal ideation does not seem to have increased among people with cannabis use disorder, despite all this legal and social change," explained Goldman-Mellor. Yet, "people with cannabis use disorder are still at a very substantially increased likelihood of experiencing serious suicidal thoughts, and that's not something that is widely understood."

The researchers stress that these findings should not be interpreted as evidence that everyone who uses marijuana faces the same elevated risk.

The study focused specifically on cannabis use disorder, a condition in which people have difficulty controlling their marijuana consumption even when it causes problems in their lives. Someone with the disorder may continue using cannabis despite harmful consequences or repeated attempts to cut back.

This distinction is important because problematic cannabis use differs from occasional or otherwise nonproblematic consumption.

The findings also do not establish that cannabis use disorder directly causes suicidal thoughts. Because the research identified an association rather than a cause-and-effect relationship, it cannot determine whether problematic cannabis use contributes to suicidal thinking, whether underlying mental health difficulties contribute to both conditions, or whether other factors help explain the connection.

Nevertheless, the results point to a significant mental health concern that deserves greater recognition, particularly among people seeking help for problematic cannabis use.

Researchers Urge Greater Mental Health Screening

One practical implication is that health care professionals should look beyond cannabis consumption itself when evaluating patients with cannabis use disorder.

Rather than focusing exclusively on depression or substance use symptoms, clinicians may benefit from asking patients directly about suicidal thoughts as part of a broader mental health assessment. This could help identify people who need additional care but whose struggles might otherwise remain unnoticed.

"Someone seeking help for cannabis use disorder may also be experiencing suicidal thoughts that are not immediately apparent," said Oyetunji. "The goal is not to assume that everyone with cannabis use disorder is suicidal but to identify those who may need additional assessment, treatment, or support."

The study arrives at a time when marijuana is increasingly viewed as a relatively low-risk substance. Public perceptions have shifted considerably, and negative attitudes toward cannabis have declined alongside expanding legalization and social acceptance.

However, these changes have not eliminated the mental health challenges associated with cannabis use disorder. Even though the strength of the association with suicidal thoughts did not increase over the study period, the elevated odds remained substantial.

The researchers suggest that health care providers, policymakers, and community organizations can play an important role by improving awareness, identifying vulnerable individuals, and making appropriate mental health support more accessible.

As attitudes toward marijuana continue to evolve, the findings serve as a reminder that the needs of people experiencing problematic cannabis use should remain a public health priority.

Said Oyetunji, "As cannabis becomes more accessible and socially accepted, we should ensure that the people struggling with its use are not overlooked."

Sanofi is buying the biotech Insmed for $41 billion, the companies said Tuesday, the largest biopharma acquisition in years and one that will give the French firm two new approved drugs.

#5548. 5 Exciting Ways to Invest in Real Estate

When it comes to exploring enticing investment opportunities, real estate often stands out as an excellent solution for making and growing wealth. No matter how the world around us changes, there will always be a demand for property in attractive areas. This has led countless people to diversify their portfolios over the years, buying rental properties, second homes, and even office spaces.

In recent years, as the world has continued to evolve, the marketplace for real estate investors has evolved with it. Today, people no longer need to buy and flip entire properties to make money. There are numerous tips for getting started and ways you can start your journey into the property world, and some options are actually simpler and more affordable than you might expect. Here are some of the best, most interesting ways to invest in real estate, if you want to avoid the traditional buy and flip strategy.

Not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world. The digital landscape has evolved drastically in recent years, introducing new opportunities for innovative entrepreneurs to make money buying virtual assets. As the concept of the metaverse continues to gain traction, digital real estate is growing increasingly attractive.

With digital real estate, companies purchase a section of the blockchain in a metaverse landscape, where they can build online experiences, or simply store other assets. In 2021, sales on four of the biggest metaverse platforms for real estate reached a whopping $501 million. This indicates learning how to invest in digital real estate could be a worthwhile strategy for any consumer. Not only is it potentially profitable, but the digital real estate also requires less work to manage and maintain than a physical house or property.

Even if you’re not familiar with this form of property-based investing, you probably know the term crowdfunding. Made popular by sites like GoFundMe and Kickstarter, the crowdfunding strategy involves individuals pooling their resources together to fund a product or business. In the real estate world, investors can work together to purchase a property, such as a corporate space, warehouse, or block of flats, reducing the initial cost of a purchase.

The approach allows investors to participate in products that would have been impossible to access in the past because of high capital requirements. Individuals can use this strategy to diversify their portfolios with a variety of different locations and property types. Plus, you’ll earn a passive income through rental profits, and property appreciation.

Another real estate investment strategy gaining increasing attention in recent years is REITs. These are basically investment vehicles responsible for owning and operating income-generating assets, such as rental properties and office blocks. They’re traded on traditional stock exchanges and provide individuals with an opportunity to invest in the market, without directly owning a property or having to manage the investment themselves.

REITs can come with several attractive features, including regular distributions of dividends, and the ability to explore a range of different sectors. You can even use this strategy to spread your portfolio across industrial, residential, and commercial properties. They’re also a highly liquid investment option, making them appealing to beginners.

Finally, one interesting way to invest in real estate, without buying a physical property outright, is to spend some of your money on shares in PropTech startups. PropTech, or Property Technology startups, are companies focused on developing tools and real estate designed to transform the property landscape. They develop things like property management solutions, smart home technology, and virtual reality applications for tours.

If you already have experience in the world of stocks and shares, investing in a PropTech company could be an excellent way to utilize your existing knowledge and diversify your portfolio. It’s also a chance to get your foot in the door with a company that’s actively disrupting the real estate space, and the market as we know it.

Investing in property has become a much more diverse and versatile opportunity for individuals in recent years. No matter how much money you can afford to spend, or where your expertise lies, you can find plenty of ways to expand your portfolio with disruptive real-estate investment strategies.

#5547. Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.

Brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism. Although adults with and without autism showed remarkably similar brain activity when researchers compared group averages, a closer examination uncovered striking differences between individuals. These differences were especially pronounced in brain regions involved in understanding and responding to social information.

The findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal important differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The discovery could help scientists better understand why autism varies so widely from person to person and eventually support more personalized approaches to care.

The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.

What Brain Scans Reveal When People Watch Movies

To explore these differences, the team examined previously collected brain imaging data from Indiana University and Caltech. The recordings captured brain activity as adults with and without autism watched movies from several genres, including animation, action, romantic comedy, and Hitchcockian thrillers.

Movies offered researchers a way to study how the brain responds to a constantly changing stream of sights, sounds, and social interactions. Unlike simple laboratory tasks, movies present a rich mixture of information that more closely resembles the complexity of everyday experiences.

Using the imaging data, the researchers trained a computational model to identify connections between brain activity and different elements of the movies. These included visual details, sounds, and more abstract social information, such as interactions between characters.

After training, the model was able to accurately predict activity across several brain systems.

Kliemann explained why this approach is particularly useful for investigating the social challenges sometimes associated with autism: "The computational model allowed us to look for robust brain responses to many different aspects of the complex, dynamic contexts in the movies."

A Surprising Difference Hidden by Brain Activity Averages

The most unexpected finding emerged when researchers compared the two groups.

At first, the results suggested relatively little difference. When brain responses were averaged across participants, the model predicted activity in various brain systems similarly for adults with and without autism.

However, the picture changed when the researchers examined how much individual participants differed from others in their own group.

People with autism showed substantially greater variation in their brain responses than participants without autism. In other words, although the overall group averages looked similar, the responses of individual autistic participants were much less alike.

This increased variability appeared across nearly every brain system examined. The strongest differences occurred in the social brain system, a network of regions involved in processing social information and understanding other people.

Why the Findings Could Change Autism Research

The results raise important questions about how scientists investigate autism. Many existing approaches to understanding and treating the condition rely heavily on comparing average measurements from groups of autistic and nonautistic individuals.

But if autistic people show considerable differences in how their brains process information, these averages may obscure some of the most meaningful findings.

Traer described the team's surprise: "We were surprised by the similarity of group averages. The results suggest that we need to focus on understanding the details of individual brain responses. How and why do they differ?"

Rather than searching only for brain activity patterns shared by everyone with autism, the findings point toward the potential value of studying individuals and identifying smaller groups with similar characteristics.

Kliemann highlighted what this could mean for future research and support: "Identifying ASD subgroups may help us build a more precise understanding of the condition and help develop ways to provide individually tailored support."

The researchers now plan to investigate how these differences in brain activity relate to variations in autism-related behavior. They hope to determine where and when the differences emerge, how they are connected to individual characteristics, and what might explain them.

Ultimately, the findings suggest that understanding autism may require looking beyond the average brain and paying closer attention to the distinctive ways individuals process the world.

#5546. How artificial intelligence is offering new hope for stroke patients in the Last Frontier

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Katie covers the impact of health technology on patients, clinicians, and businesses. Her stories explore the price tag of clinical AI, digital health at the FDA, and the boom in direct-to-consumer telehealth. Confidential tips can be sent on Signal at palmer.01.

It was just after lunchtime when the doctor’s phone started to vibrate and chime. On this summer Wednesday, a neurointerventionalist in Anchorage got the alert: Three hundred miles away, at a hospital deep in Alaska’s interior, a clot in a major artery was blocking the flow of blood to a patient’s brain. He needed it out — and he’d have to come to the state’s biggest city to get it done.

Time is never on a stroke patient’s side. Every minute without blood flow, 2 million brain cells die. And in Alaska — a state more than double the size of Texas, most of it inaccessible by road — it can take several hours to arrange a plane, airlift a patient to Ted Stevens airport in Anchorage, and deliver them by ambulance to one of the five neurointerventionalists in the entire state who can extract clots.

In his mid-60s, the patient on the doctor’s phone had arrived at a nearby emergency room after a morning fall, suddenly weak on his left side. Like most patients with stroke symptoms, he got a head CT, which helps diagnose a stroke, whether it’s caused by a clot or a brain bleed, and determine whether that clot can be broken up with drugs or needs to be extracted. Normally, once the scan is complete, it could take 45 precious minutes just to send those thousands of two-dimensional brain snapshots to Anchorage for review — 90 million brain cells before a doctor could accept his transfer.

But this summer day, the patient had a new type of technology on his team. Stroke is the fourth-leading cause of death in the United States, the majority caused by occlusions that block blood flow to the brain, and survival rates are significantly worse for rural patients. In recent years, states have built up stroke networks, including telestroke care and automated artificial intelligence analysis, to try to improve transfer times for patients without access to specialist neurological care. One of the latest additions was in Alaska — where, starting in 2023, a small network of hospitals had agreed to use the same AI software to triage stroke patients and get them to the right care, faster.

Nearly instantly, the tool, from RapidAI, analyzed his CT scan for signs of a large vessel occlusion, or LVO, a type of blockage that often needs to be mechanically sucked out or retrieved with a stent. Through an app used by other hospitals with the technology, the results went out to his local team of doctors and the faraway network of neurointerventionalists — one of whom was on call at Providence Alaska Medical Center in Anchorage.

The app alerted the doctor with the results just seconds after the scan was complete: suspected LVO. Less than a half hour after the patient arrived at his local ER, the team had called Providence for a transfer — two minutes before their on-call radiologist even delivered their official CT report.

Four hours and 23 minutes later, the clot was out. Without the AI assist, it would have taken at least an extra hour.

In 2026, it’s not rare for a hospital to use AI to triage stroke patients. Eight years ago, clinical trials showed that automated image analysis could extend the clot removal window for stroke patients as late as 24 hours after they were last well — before this, the window was just six hours. At the same time, the Food and Drug Administration approved the first AI to detect large vessel occlusions.

Those “were the wonder years,” said Stanford neurologist Greg Albers, co-founder of RapidAI. “Stroke centers scrambled to access the software.” Developers started to bundle different stroke algorithms in one package, driven by vendors like Viz.ai, Aidoc, and Brainomix, along with RapidAI.

As with most new medical technology, though, that adoption has been uneven. At the forefront of the deployment were large metropolitan hospitals, including those categorized as comprehensive stroke centers.

“Maybe it’s because they had more advanced workflows in place. Maybe it’s because they had the funding to acquire this AI software,” said Casey Pelzl, a researcher at the Harvey L. Neiman Health Policy Institution who studied some of the technology’s early adoption. “But what we know about stroke is that a lot of patients seek initial treatment at noncomprehensive stroke care centers, and these are the places that could potentially benefit from it the most.”

That’s the promise that a small group of stroke coordinators and neurointerventionalists in Alaska saw in 2023, when they established a volunteer nonprofit called the Alaska Stroke Coalition in a bid to improve stroke outcomes in a state that throws up obstacles at every turn.

“The distances that we have to cross are enormous. The weather that we have to face is awful. Resource availability is so low,” said Kelly Isaacs, Providence’s stroke program manager. Sometimes Alaskans arrive at their village clinics by snow machine or dogsled. The state doesn’t have consistent reporting of stroke outcomes. And in the summer months, when cruise ships wind up the coast, a seaside hub’s population can swell nearly tenfold, often enriched with older passengers. Jaded hospital workers sometimes call them the “stroke boats.”

Against those unfavorable odds, one thing that could improve patients’ chances of survival after a stroke is getting them to the right care as fast as possible. “‘Time is brain’ is still very much the case, and the more quickly you can start a treatment — whether it’s the drug to break up the clot or if it’s a big clot, to transport them where they can get the clot taken out — that’s going to make a big difference for people,” said UC Health neurologist and stroke researcher Joseph Broderick.

By 2023, a few hospitals in the state, mostly in Anchorage, had started using RapidAI’s software, but barely any regional hospitals in the state’s interior and on its far-flung coasts did. Even for those hospitals that had the tech, “the challenge was we existed in all these different systems, but we weren’t coordinated,” said David Stoffel, RapidAI’s chief business officer. Each hospital had its own software license and didn’t share information within the app, making it difficult to coordinate decision-making for patients who might have needed a transfer.

So the newly formed Alaska Stroke Coalition, whose founders included Isaacs, tried to build a solution. Lucy He, a neurointerventionalist in Alaska, found funding from a family foundation to buy RapidAI for six additional hospitals spread across the state, at a cost of about $450,000. The resulting network spread from Alaska’s very northernmost tip in Utqiagvik, all the way south to the state’s capital of Juneau, which can only be accessed by air or water. When the tech threw up an alert about possible LVO in a patient, the message wouldn’t just circulate within that hospital team — it would go out wide, to the neurointerventionalists in Anchorage who might be able to help.

In return for the coalition paying for the AI tool, the health systems agreed to report their performance over the next three years, to see if the technology could really make a difference.

Day to day, the stroke coordinators and doctors accepting patients from across the state saw the technology changing their decision-making. It wasn’t always about quickly transferring patients for treatment — sometimes it was about making the hard calls to stay put.

Kevin Myrick, one of the coalition’s founders and Providence’s stroke program coordinator, pointed to a patient transferred to Providence this summer: a man in his 80s with a large vessel occlusion and severe symptoms. Patients like him are usually paralyzed on one side and lose speech. When strokes are this bad, it is far from given that a patient will regain function after treatment: Dead brain tissue is dead, forever. And restoring blood flow to dead tissue can do more harm than good, reintroducing toxic metabolic byproducts into circulation and causing swelling and bleeding.

“We did not put this [technology] in to transfer every patient to Anchorage,” said Myrick. If a patient doesn’t have enough chance for recovery, it can be preferable to keep them closer to home — to save them expense, keep them near their support network, and avoid using limited EMS staff time and planes.

In these cases, it’s a head CT with a contrast agent showing detailed blood flow in the brain that can help doctors tell what intervention is worthwhile. In the Rapid app, that image looks like a series of brain slices colored in neon-bright, Lisa Frank shades of green and pink. Pink tissue is gone. Green is brain that has the potential to be salvaged if blood flow is restored in time. “In Alaska, where you’ve got those big distances, having that imaging is going to be really important about deciding who to send and why to send,” said Broderick, of UC Health.

For the patient in his 80s, the CT perfusion images that came through the app showed far more green tissue than pink, their volumes neatly tabulated in milliliters by the software. “This patient was definitely a go,” said Myrick. He traveled 750 miles — about the distance from New York City to Chicago — and within a few minutes of arrival was shuttled into Providence’s catheterization lab, its team ready and waiting.

A CT scan after the clot removal shows his brain in profile. Blood fills the main arteries and tangled branches that supply oxygen throughout the entire brain; in his first CT, nearly half of that field was blank, its roadways cut off by the clot. Still weak and with impaired speech after the mechanical thrombectomy, he has a long way to go, said Isaacs. But “when he got sent home, he’s got a much better chance of recovery than he would have otherwise.”

The technology isn’t perfect. Like most radiology algorithms, there are false positives — scans that the app will say show a large vessel occlusion that actually don’t. It takes a good image to work well, said Broderick: “Sometimes, when you look at the pictures, if the person moves or the study wasn’t done right, the data is not good.” That means a doctor still reviews every output, and that official read is what drives the call to transfer or not. And for the biggest returns, it requires a hospital to actually perform CT perfusion imaging, which hasn’t been uniformly adopted in hospitals that don’t remove clots themselves.

But despite the limitations, the hospitals that have received the technology through the coalition’s grant are enthusiastic about connecting more of Alaska with the same alert system. “In rural Alaska, at all these tribal health organization hospitals, I think that that really can change the narrative here,” said Dylan Latif, stroke coordinator at Alaska Native Medical Center, one of the program’s grantees, at a meeting of the coalition in early October.

“If we do this with a bunch of different hospitals, then we create, you know, the Skynet of stroke in Alaska,” said He, the neurointerventionalist, at the same meeting.

The stroke coalition hasn’t yet published research about how the technology has impacted stroke care for Alaskans. But early data point to a recent increase in the number of thrombectomies delivered in Alaska, which could be driven in part by the program. And once patients arrived in Anchorage, hospitals with cath labs saw about a 30% improvement in the time it takes to start threading a device in to retrieve a clot.

“Logistically, every cath lab in America during normal business hours is booked 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. all day, every day,” Isaacs explained. With coordinated alerts from referring hospitals, it can be easier to prepare for stroke patients’ arrival. “We’ve got our little flight tracker up, and we’re like, OK, they’re 30 minutes out,” she said.

As is so often the case with AI deployed in health care, it will be longer before Alaska can show whether the new technology is changing the outcomes that matter the most: rates of long-term disability and death from strokes. It’s especially challenging in Alaska, where detailed data has been scarce; more complete stroke intervention and outcome recording began at the same time the coalition expanded the use of AI.

“Can I give you statistically significant information that RapidAI has made a big difference in the state of Alaska?” said Isaacs. “I can’t, really.”

For now, some doctors who care for stroke patients in Alaska are optimistic. “Being able to take these people who are from way the heck out of the middle of nowhere, they got 45 minutes to the local scanner, and now they are deemed eligible for an intervention — it has saved countless numbers of patients,” said Ryan Wilson, a neurologist at Alaska Native Medical Center, to his colleagues during the October meeting. “They’re gaining their brain back.”

As the members of the Alaska Stroke Coalition face down the end of their three-year grant period, that enthusiasm is translating into action: Each one of the six hospitals that got free access to RapidAI has said it wants to keep and pay for it. And there’s hope for even more significant changes to the landscape of stroke care in the state.

“Coincidentally, three things happened that help us further that mission,” said Isaacs.

The first happened this February, when the American Heart Association and the American Stroke Association released new stroke guidelines. The previous guidelines suggested narrow windows in which a patient could be treated with clot-busting drugs: They had 4 1/2 hours to get the medication. But in the updated guidelines, depending on how much salvageable tissue a patient appears to have in one of those pink-and-green CT perfusion images, they can still receive the drugs nine, even 24 hours after symptoms started.

That could dramatically increase the number of treatable stroke patients in Alaska — especially those who can be treated in place by clot-busting drugs. With RapidAI in more hospitals, Isaacs hopes that perfusion imaging will become more common, helping to make those calls about whether a patient falls in those extended windows. “Stroke used to be way more depressing to take care of, because our treatment options were very limited,” she said. “The windows were very short, and now with increased technology and increased time in our guidelines, it’s not quite as sad as it used to be, honestly.”

The second boost came in June, when Alaska enacted a law that will help establish statewide standards for strokes and heart attacks, like it already had in place for trauma. “We always sort of looked over at what trauma had, and we were like, ‘Isn’t that great? They’ve got designations, they get site visits, they’ve got data collection. We need these things,’” said Isaacs, who, along with several other coalition members, voiced support for the bill.

And in October, the final piece of the puzzle fell into place: The coalition got word that the work it’s been doing is primed to expand. “They got proof of concept that they can achieve this equity of care in Alaska for stroke,” said RapidAI’s Stoffel, and leveraged it in an application to the five-year, $50 billion federal Rural Health Transformation Program.

In the first year of funding, the Alaska Stroke Coalition received $3.2 million of the state’s funding to start building a statewide AI imaging network.

With grant-funded hospitals and independent purchases combined, Alaska will soon have 21 acute care hospitals and two CT scan-enabled clinics with RapidAI’s stroke system in place. “This is phenomenal for Alaska,” said RapidAI’s Albers. “There are financial issues for some of these smaller hospitals, and I think they’re even more significant in Alaska than elsewhere.”

The group hopes to receive funding for at least two more years — first, to build support infrastructure that allows for rapid decisions to transfer or keep patients, and then track the financial impact of the technology on hospitals.

“As a girl who was born and raised in Alaska, this is the most Alaskan story that you can get,” Isaacs said to the room of her colleagues in the coalition’s October meeting. Earlier that day, she had gotten the email confirming the grant funding. “It’s like, ‘Oh, you don’t want to do it? Fine, we’ll go do it ourselves.’ And here we are.”

#5545. If the AI Bubble Pops, Here’s What It Means for Your Home’s Value

When artificial intelligence giant Anthropic went public last week, its $1.494 trillion valuation exceeded the combined value of every owner-occupied home in the San Francisco metropolitan area, according to research from Realtor.com®.

Less than a week later, the company's shares fell below their IPO price, as a renewed sell-off in tech stocks stoked fears that the AI bubble may already be bursting.

“This is how the exuberance ends—not with a whimper but with a bang,” Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman wrote on Monday.

Krugman, who warned of America's housing bubble as early as 2005, acknowledges he's less certain about AI valuations than he was about home prices two decades ago. But earlier this month, he warned that an AI bust would almost certainly trigger a recession, potentially more painful than the one that followed the dot-com crash.

Others on Wall Street aren't so sure. Many investors remain confident in the industry's fundamentals and see the sell-off as a necessary correction rather than the end of the boom.

But after years of a bull market powered by a handful of AI darlings, new research from Realtor.com finds evidence that the resulting fortunes have helped shape some of America’s most expensive housing markets.

Now, a reversal of those gains could threaten a source of wealth far more central to the financial lives of middle-class Americans: their homes.

Anthropic's IPO alone was expected to mint around 2,800 millionaires among its current and former employees, according to estimates from private-market research firm Sacra reported by Reuters.

But Americans needn't work in AI or invest in individual tech stocks to have shared in the windfall. Between the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022 and Nov. 3 of this year, the S&P 500 gained nearly $32 trillion in market value—more than half of which came from just 10 AI-linked companies, according to Bloomberg.

About 62% of Americans own stocks, either directly or through investments such as retirement accounts, according to a 2025 Gallup poll. Yet the wealthiest 10% of households hold 88% of the country's household stocks and mutual fund assets.

In the San Francisco Bay Area's AI hubs, some of that AI-powered stock wealth has translated into an estimated $61,180 in additional down payment on a typical home, according to research from Realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu. At the entry-level luxury tier, that premium reached nearly $200,000 in 2025.

The extra cash these buyers have brought to the market has allowed them to bid higher without taking on more debt, potentially displacing competitors into less expensive price brackets and driving up competition further down the market, Xu's earlier research suggests.

And so, what’s a barrier to entry for prospective buyers becomes a source of equity gains for existing homeowners—even those who have never invested in AI.

Annual home price growth now exceeds the national rate in all three markets where Xu identified signs of AI wealth bolstering down payments: Chicago (6.9%), New York City (5.8%), and San Francisco (3.7%), compared with 2.1% nationally, according to Tuesday's Case-Shiller release.

It’s an especially important point to make here because real estate wealth is more widely distributed than stock. Households between the 50th and 90th wealth percentiles hold nearly half of the country's household real estate assets, but just 11.4% of its stocks and mutual fund shares, according to second-quarter Federal Reserve data.

Homeowners in markets buoyed by AI wealth have, in effect, acquired a stake in the industry's stock market performance—whether or not they own any shares.

And the potential losses are enormous. To gauge their scale, Krugman looks to the so-called Buffett indicator, which measures the total value of U.S. stocks relative to the country's gross domestic product.

Before the recent sell-off, the ratio had climbed well above its peak during the dot-com bubble. AI-related companies accounted for nearly half of the S&P 500's market value and drove most of the increase in the indicator over the past several years, Krugman explains.

“If the Buffett indicator falls back to what it was in, say, 2019, that would wipe out wealth equal to around 80 percent of GDP: $25 trillion,” he wrote.

And if his warning seems alarmist, consider what he wrote about the U.S. housing market in August 2005: “This is the way the bubble ends: not with a pop, but with a hiss.”

More than two years before the onset of the Great Recession, Krugman identified falling sales and rising inventory as the early signs of a housing bust, as sellers struggled to command prices that buyers were no longer willing to pay.

Some of those symptoms are present today. In October, contract signings fell 17% annually while inventory grew 7.4%. Asking prices recorded their 12th consecutive month of annual declines, according to Realtor.com research.

But the slowdown predates November's sell-off. Elevated mortgage rates and years of home price growth that outpaced wages have driven buyers to the sidelines, while many homeowners can afford to wait for better offers.

“On the seller side, we see more of a pause than an exodus,” Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com, said earlier this month.

The question is whether an AI bust would produce another localized housing correction or a national downturn.

“Generally speaking, the stock market and housing market can be connected, but usually not directly,” Krimmel explained amid an earlier bout of AI stock volatility in November 2025. “If they're moving together, that's typically because of some other outside force (could be driven by policy, Fed moves, and credit conditions, or a large macro shock) and/or because of changes in the job market.”

To his point, when the dot-com bubble burst, the Nasdaq plunged more than 75% from its peak, wiping out trillions in paper wealth. Yet national home values continued to climb through the 2001 recession.

In San Francisco, however, home values fell 6.1% between February 2001 and January 2002, even as they rose 6% nationally, according to an analysis of seasonally adjusted Case-Shiller home price data.

The bigger question hanging over the housing market, though, is what an AI bust would mean for household spending.

When households lose stock market wealth, they tend to spend less, even if their paychecks haven't changed—a phenomenon economists call the wealth effect. And just as stock market gains have held up demand for homes, they've also helped sustain demand elsewhere in the economy.

Any resulting pullback in spending, therefore, could end up rippling into layoffs in industries far removed from AI. Likewise, a slowdown in AI infrastructure investment could compound those losses, jeopardizing construction and manufacturing jobs in communities distant from Silicon Valley.

“Labor market softness is key for aggregate (and housing) demand,” Krimmel said last year.

And while the destruction of stock market wealth might initially dampen housing demand in a handful of affluent markets, rising unemployment could weaken it nationwide.

During the dot-com bust, the Federal Reserve cut interest rates aggressively, helping sustain housing demand despite the economic downturn. Persistent inflation could complicate a similar response today.

“Lower interest rates will, in theory, help struggling companies' finances and allow them to keep existing workers, hire more, and/or provide pay raises to top performers,” Krimmel explained last November.

Access to credit could also become a problem. Tech companies are relying more heavily on corporate debt and private credit to finance their expansion, according to the European Central Bank's November Financial Stability Review. Losses on those investments could prompt lenders to tighten credit, making financing harder to obtain for homebuyers and builders alike.

The combination of falling incomes and more restrictive lending could depress home values in markets where AI wealth never drove them up in the first place.

But unlike during the Great Recession, a decline in home values would leave far fewer homeowners owing more than their properties are worth, limiting the risk of widespread foreclosures and the additional downward pressure on prices that forced sales can create.

“The typical homeowner today—and the housing market overall—is still well-positioned to withstand a correction without it turning into a crisis,” Krimmel said last November. “Home equity hit an all-time high in 2025Q2; mortgage holders are largely locked into sub-4% rates, giving them lower payments that are increasingly being eaten away by inflation. Very few homeowners are at risk of going underwater, even if prices were to decline 10% to 15%.”

A year later, homeowner equity cushions remain substantial and mortgage delinquencies are low by historical standards, according to the Fed's November Financial Stability Report.

“Obviously, [a stock market crash] is not something anyone wants to see play out, and undoubtedly, if a stock market correction spilled over into the housing market, many homeowners would feel the pain,” Krimmel said. “The silver lining of that hypothetical is that the knock-on effects would not be as severe. Luckily, the history of the housing bust and Great Recession would not repeat itself.”

But for tens of millions of families, home equity is the college fund, the retirement plan, the safety net, and the most important source of wealth they'll ever build. The financial protections that could keep them in their homes during a downturn wouldn't necessarily protect that wealth.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5544. Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of NetApp INSIGHT

Intelligent data infrastructure is becoming a priority as enterprises move artificial intelligence beyond isolated pilots and into production environments.

The shift places new demands on storage systems built to support traditional applications, especially as organizations introduce AI workloads across hybrid and multicloud environments. NetApp Inc. is responding with a strategy that emphasizes infrastructure modernization without requiring enterprises to abandon existing investments, according to George Kurian (pictured), chief executive officer of NetApp.

“I think that the AI era requires organizations to be really good stewards of their data, because data is the foundation for knowledge and knowledge is the intellectual property,” he told theCUBE. “To have knowledge, you need really good intelligent data infrastructure that not only allows you to extract memory and context from your data, but also to keep it secure, well governed and a resource that you can trust.”

Kurian spoke with theCUBE Research’s Christophe Bertrand and co-host Rebecca Knight during NetApp INSIGHT, in an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. The event’s coverage featured NetApp executives and technology partners discussing the evolving demands on enterprise data infrastructure and the challenges of bringing AI into production. (Disclosure below.)

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with George Kurian:

Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of NetApp INSIGHT:

Enterprise AI workloads are exposing limitations in storage architectures designed for more predictable application demands. NetApp’s Novus architecture separates data and metadata management so each can scale independently. The company’s AI Data Engine is designed to discover, classify and prepare enterprise data for AI applications, according to Syam Nair, chief product officer of NetApp.

“Performance and throughput of accessing the data, that’s a necessity for AI, but that won’t be sufficient for agents to actually act on the data,” he said during the event. “If the data is not ready and it’s not protected, you get fast results. You get compromised results, but they may not be the ones you want.”

The demands of AI factories are also changing how storage resources must be managed. NetApp’s approach aims to support high-throughput AI pipelines without sacrificing the responsiveness other applications require, according to Arindam Banerjee, chief platform and technology officer of NetApp, who spoke alongside Jason Hardy, vice president of storage technology at Nvidia Corp.

“What happens is [that] different types of workloads like transactional workloads for metadata and heavy sequential workloads for, say, checkpoints, happen at the same time,” Banerjee told theCUBE. “Previous architectures did one or the other very well. They never were able to combine it and do both at the same time.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Jason Hardy and Arindam Banerjee:

Modernizing enterprise infrastructure often requires organizations to accommodate existing applications while introducing new AI capabilities. NetApp and Oracle Corp. are addressing that challenge through a co-engineered, fully managed storage service that runs ONTAP natively within Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The offering is designed to ease migration of existing ONTAP workloads without requiring application redesign, according to Konstantinos Papamiltiadis, senior vice president of partnerships at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, a division of Oracle.

“When I’m going into the OCI console, I have the option to use the ONTAP as a native service,” he told theCUBE. “For me, the most important thing that we managed to build is, from an operational perspective, we bring everything under one single interface that provides simplicity and consistency.”

NetApp and Oracle Corp. are extending enterprise storage capabilities into the public cloud through a co-engineered, fully managed service that runs ONTAP natively within Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The offering is designed to ease migration of existing ONTAP workloads without requiring application redesign, according to Konstantinos Papamiltiadis, senior vice president of partnerships at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, a division of Oracle.

“When I’m going into the OCI console, I have the option to use the ONTAP as a native service,” he told theCUBE. “For me, the most important thing that we managed to build is, from an operational perspective, we bring everything under one single interface that provides simplicity and consistency.”

The integration challenge extends beyond cloud storage to the networking and compute resources that support AI workloads. NetApp and Cisco Systems Inc. are expanding their FlexPod infrastructure with validated designs intended to reduce deployment complexity. The partnership has served 10,000 customers over 16 years, according to James Cole, vice president of data center networking, business development, partnerships and go-to-market at Cisco, and Alvaro Celis, chief partner and ecosystem officer at NetApp.

“Twenty years ago, 10 years ago, you would’ve been designing your data structures and your applications around the infrastructure. Now we’ve turned that on its head,” Cole said during the event. “You’re really designing the infrastructure around the movement of data. Who better to do that together than the person you trust with your data and the person you trust with your network?”

Another partnership focuses on private AI deployment and measurable business outcomes. The NetApp AIPod Mini combines NetApp infrastructure with the Generate platform from Iterate Studio Inc., doing business as Iterate.ai, according to Brian Sathianathan, co-founder and chief technology officer of Iterate.ai. In one insurance deployment cited during the discussion, an agent reduced accident-report analysis from approximately eight hours to eight minutes.

“AIPod Mini has attached connections to the NetApp storage, and it talks to NetApp using the ONTAP protocol that’s time-tested,” he said during the event. “Then, on top of the AIPod Mini, we are running our Generate software. That software has a [large language model] embedded in it, so you can run all your AI queries locally and fully privately within your four walls.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Alvaro Celis and James Cole:

As enterprises introduce autonomous agents into infrastructure management, intelligent data infrastructure must accommodate increasingly complex operational demands. NetApp’s unified control plane, delivered through NetApp Console, is designed to reduce routine administrative work through policy-driven automation. In one keynote demonstration, agents responded to a nighttime performance anomaly, according to Sandeep Singh, senior vice president and general manager of enterprise storage at NetApp.

“Agents can, in real time, implement the necessary quality of service rules to ensure there’s compliance to the boundary conditions there,” he told theCUBE. “And that way, no human is woken up. The right outcome is achieved, and there’s no noisy neighbor effect. And there’s an audit trail presented to the humans for going and following up.”

Automation, however, can’t resolve organizational questions about data ownership and responsibility. As enterprises extend intelligent data infrastructure across applications and environments, leadership must establish accountability for the information those systems rely on, according to Helen Yu, founder and chief executive officer of Tigon Advisory Corp., who appeared alongside Singh.

“It’s not a storage problem. It’s a leadership and accountability issue,” she said during the event. “When teams don’t have access to … trusted data consistently, they actually stop making decisions. They start making workarounds.”

#5542. Tiny magnets deep inside the brain could transform Parkinson’s treatment

An international research team has developed a new technique that uses magnetic fields and tiny particles to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, potentially opening the door to a less invasive treatment for Parkinson's disease. In experiments involving mice with Parkinson's-like symptoms, the approach significantly improved movement problems without requiring permanently implanted electrodes.

The technique involves injecting specially designed magnetic nanoplatelets into a targeted area of the brain. When exposed to an external magnetic field, these particles generate tiny forces that activate nearby nerve cells. Unlike conventional brain stimulation treatments, which rely on surgically implanted electrodes, the new approach uses magnetic forces to influence brain activity. The findings, published in Advanced Science, come from researchers at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU), RWTH Aachen, and the Universities of Maastricht (the Netherlands) and Leuven (Belgium).

Why Parkinson's Treatment Often Requires Brain Implants

Parkinson's disease develops as brain cells responsible for producing dopamine gradually break down. Dopamine is a chemical messenger that plays a vital role in controlling movement. As its levels decline, communication within the brain's movement circuits becomes disrupted, contributing to tremors and other motor difficulties.

For some patients, deep brain stimulation can help control these symptoms. This treatment uses a device known as a brain pacemaker, which is implanted beneath the collarbone and connected to electrodes placed deep inside the brain. The electrodes deliver electrical stimulation to a region called the subthalamic nucleus (STN for short), helping to modify abnormal activity in the brain circuits responsible for movement.

Although this treatment can provide substantial relief, it requires a complex surgical procedure and does not work for everyone.

"The procedure is relatively complex, however, and not always successful," explains Prof. Dr. Danijela Gregurec from the Department of Chemistry and Pharmacy at FAU. "This puts many Parkinson's patients off, and not all patients are suitable candidates for one of these pacemakers."

The researchers believe magnetic stimulation could eventually provide another option, allowing doctors to influence the same deep brain structures without leaving electrodes permanently implanted.

How Tiny Magnetic Particles Stimulate Brain Cells

The new technology takes advantage of the ability of certain nerve cells to detect physical pressure and mechanical forces.

"We use magnetic nanoparticles that we implant in the brain," Gregurec explains. "They have a special shape and a magnetic structure. They were developed in order to transform magnetic fields into tiny mechanical forces."

Rather than sending electrical pulses directly into the brain, the technique uses these particles to produce extremely small physical movements when a magnetic field is applied.

"The traditional method establishes an electrical connection to the brain," she says. "In contrast, we use the neurons' natural mechanosensors to influence regions deep within the brain."

The process works by gently changing the shape of nearby nerve cell membranes. Imagine pressing a finger against an inflated balloon and creating a small indentation in its surface. The magnetic particles produce a similar effect on a microscopic scale.

This slight deformation opens specialized channels in the cell membrane that respond to mechanical pressure. Once opened, these channels allow electrically charged particles called ions to enter the nerve cells, changing their electrical activity and providing a way to stimulate the targeted brain circuits.

Magnetic Brain Stimulation Improves Movement in Mice

To investigate whether the technology could relieve Parkinson's symptoms, the international research team conducted experiments using mice with damage to the same types of dopamine-producing nerve cells affected by the disease in humans. This damage caused movement difficulties resembling those seen in Parkinson's patients.

"Together with our partners from Maastricht, we injected magnetic nanoparticles developed here at FAU into the animals' subthalamic nucleus," Gregurec explains. "That is the very region in the brain that is also an important target for conventional deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease."

The researchers used precise stereotactic injection techniques to deliver the particles to the intended location. These methods rely on carefully calculated three-dimensional coordinates to guide instruments into specific brain structures. Accurate placement was particularly important because the treatment needed to affect the correct neural circuits involved in movement.

After the particles were positioned, the researchers applied an external magnetic field. The results were encouraging: the mice showed significant improvements in their movement deficits.

"The effect is roughly equivalent to what we would have expected after implanting a brain pacemaker," says Gregurec.

The findings suggest that magnetic nanoparticles could provide a different way to achieve some of the benefits of conventional deep brain stimulation, without the need for permanently implanted electrodes.

Could Future Parkinson's Treatments Use Magnetic Headbands?

Another encouraging finding involved how the brain responded to the implanted particles over time. The magnetic nanoparticles remained in place throughout an observation period lasting several months, and the researchers found no signs of inflammation. This suggests that the particles were well tolerated during the experiments.

However, delivering the particles still required an injection directly into the brain. Gregurec and her colleagues are now investigating ways to make the procedure even less invasive.

One possibility is to develop particles that could be injected into the bloodstream and then travel into the brain by crossing the blood-brain barrier. This protective boundary normally prevents many substances circulating in the blood from entering brain tissue. Finding a way to deliver the particles across it could eliminate the need for direct brain injections.

The researchers are also exploring compact wearable devices capable of generating the magnetic fields needed for stimulation. One possibility is a headband that patients could put on themselves, potentially making treatment more convenient and adjustable.

These ideas remain at an early stage, and the researchers expect that several more years of development will be needed before the technology could be considered for clinical use.

"Nevertheless, we are convinced that the new method has enormous potential," Gregurec states. "It is not only considerably simpler and cheaper than a conventional brain pacemaker, it is probably also more flexible. Adjusting the parameters of the magnetic field would allow us to control the nanoparticles more accurately."

Beyond its potential medical applications, the technology could also become a valuable scientific tool. By allowing researchers to stimulate nerve cells through carefully controlled mechanical forces, it offers a new way to explore how physical changes at the cellular level influence brain activity.

Although the treatment has so far been demonstrated only in animals, its ability to improve movement without permanently implanted electrodes represents a promising step toward new approaches to Parkinson's disease and brain stimulation.

#5541. Opinion: Genomic testing is too fragmented. Instead, we should test once and evaluate often

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Hagman is a genetic counselor and vice president of medical affairs and strategic integration at Ambry Genetics, a Tempus company.

Genomic testing can answer a variety of pressing health questions a person (and their clinician) might face throughout their lifespan.

Unfortunately, these valuable tests have become fragmented and iterative for most patients. A patient may receive a carrier screening test before or during pregnancy; a cancer predisposition test to screen for inherited cancer-predisposition variants like BRCA, the breast cancer gene; and a pharmacogenomic test before starting a medication. Each test is a new blood draw or buccal swab, a new wet lab workflow, a new spot on a genome sequencer, a new analysis, and new costs borne by patients and insurance companies.

With the precipitous decline in the cost of whole genome sequencing, it’s time to consolidate testing by sequencing genomes once and reevaluating them when needed.

As research has shown, patients face many challenges to accessing genomic testing including financial barriers, limited access to providers, geographic limitations, and clinician biases. Since the genome can enable diagnoses and care for so many health conditions, a more streamlined and uniform approach to genomic testing would likely benefit many patients. I call it “test once, evaluate often.”

A “test once, evaluate often” approach could start at any age. For some families, that might be at birth, as an optional add-on to the newborn screening their baby already gets. A single whole genome sequence could be stored, along with other medical records information, for future analysis. Any time a clinician orders a new genomic test, the lab would simply reevaluate the relevant genes and issue a report.

This approach would dramatically lower the cost and turnaround time needed to answer genomic questions by eliminating the sample handling and wet lab processing of patient samples, potentially improving access to genomic information for patients who would otherwise choose to forgo testing due to costs.

Such a paradigm would only apply to tests looking at germline DNA (the DNA we are born with). Clinical genomic tests seeking to understand the genetics of other biological characteristics, such as somatic DNA in a cancer tissue, circulating fetal DNA in a noninvasive prenatal test, or circulating tumor DNA in liquid biopsy panels would still be needed to look for genomic variants beyond germline DNA when patient circumstances dictate.

Newborn screening is one of public health’s great successes. For more than 60 years, nearly every U.S. baby has had a heel-prick blood test for dozens of serious, treatable conditions, catching thousands of babies each year who look perfectly healthy.

For many, early diagnosis is the difference between life and death. Infants with severe combined immunodeficiency who receive a transplant by 3.5 months survive 94% of the time. Babies destined for the most severe form of spinal muscular atrophy who receive gene therapy before symptoms emerge go on to sit independently and breathe without permanent ventilation. Any interruption to newborn screening would cost children their lives.

Genome sequencing builds on that foundation. In the BabySeq Project, 9.4% of newborns had an unexpected genetic risk for childhood-onset disease. In New York’s GUARDIAN study, 72% of families opted in and 3.7% of babies screened positive, including for treatable conditions that standard screening misses. Because sequencing alone misses some cases that biochemical tests catch, it should add to the heel prick, not replace it.

In childhood, reporting can stay focused on conditions where knowing early changes care; the rest of the genome can wait until there’s a question to answer. And as with any public health program, clear consent and transparent data use must be built in from the start.

The need for genomic information changes with patient circumstances and throughout their lifespan. This is why regular evaluation of the genome is needed in place of the piecemeal approach to ordering individual tests today.

Unfortunately, genomic science is not yet in a place where a single point of evaluation is practical. Evidence about emerging gene-disease relationships and new understandings of variants associated with hereditary cancer and other diseases continue to be adopted into clinical practice, meaning that an analysis conducted 20 years into the future would likely deliver more information than is currently possible.

The genomics community has honed a version of this practice, termed reanalysis, in the rare disease space. There, it is commonplace to reexamine a patient’s exome or genome based on emerging clinical evidence about gene-disease relationships.

Reevaluation is a bit different. Reanalysis is done for the same testing indication (i.e., finding the genetic cause of a rare disease) and reevaluation is studying the same genome for a new testing indication.

The National Human Genome Research Institute envisions a future where genomic data is systematically collected and used more regularly and efficiently for patient benefit. Getting there means moving clinical and laboratory medicine toward a system in which a genome sequenced once, whether at birth or later in life, helps a person’s clinicians manage their health throughout their life.

Making this vision a reality will require several changes to the way medicine is practiced and paid for today.

First, health systems, laboratories, and policymakers need to agree on how genomic data will be stored securely for decades and who can see it. Patients already trust online patient portals with their lab results and medical records, and genomic data can be held to the same standards of security and transparency.

These questions are already being actively worked on. Leading newborn sequencing programs, such as New York’s GUARDIAN study and England’s Generation Study, ask parents for opt-in consent, keep data under strict access controls, and are studying how long it should be kept. Leftover newborn screening blood spots have also been stored for years in many states, often without parents knowing, which is why consent and transparency have become central to this work. Any program that stores genomes, at birth or later, must start with fully informed consent: patients and parents should know what is kept, where, for how long and who may use it, and be free to say no.

Second, additional genetic counseling resources would need to support patients along their genomic health journeys, helping balance clinical needs, desires for information, and the familial implications of genomic insights. That support matters even more as care becomes increasingly patient-driven, with more people ordering tests themselves, reading their own results, and coming back with new questions.

Finally, and perhaps most important, insurers need a way to pay for evaluating a genome that has already been sequenced. Today, insurance can cover reanalysis, but there is no clear path to pay for reevaluation, the step that makes “test once, evaluate often” work. Paying for it would save insurers money, too, since it could replace repeat sequencing over a patient’s lifetime. Without reimbursement for prevention-oriented sequencing, genetic counseling, and genomic evaluation, we can’t improve equity in genomic testing.

Something I’ve seen again and again in the rare disease setting is that parents of a child without a diagnosis are almost always eager to share their child’s genetic data. They know that a match with another family somewhere in the world may be what finally explains what’s happening, and many new gene discoveries start exactly that way.

If we protect genomic data well and show people what sharing makes possible, more of us may come to see it the way these parents do: not as a risk to minimize, but as a path to answers, prevention, and cures.

Kelly Hagman, M.S., is a genetic counselor and vice president of medical affairs and strategic integration at Ambry Genetics, a Tempus company. She led the launch of the industry’s first clinical exome and has authored more than 55 peer-reviewed publications.
